1.title: Assessing the System: Impact, Vendors and Proprietary Models
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Assessing the System. A system has been chosen. Before it goes live, the deployer assesses it: the impact on people, the terms of the vendor agreement, and, when the company builds its own model, the extra duties and liability that follow. This is the second competency of domain four.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Carry out or check an impact assessment of the chosen system. Identify and weigh the key terms and risks of a vendor or license agreement. See what running your own proprietary model gains and costs. And know when a deployer becomes a provider, and what follows.

1.title: Case Check-In: The Chosen Assistant, the Contract and an In-House Idea
1.text: At Helios, Samira Haddad asks for an impact assessment on the chosen assistant, not the design-stage one. Ravi Menon and Jonas Weber review the Corvid Labs agreement: data use, indemnity and notice of model changes. Then a proposal appears: build an in-house model. Samira Haddad asks what that would change. Your task is to assess the system, weigh the contract, and compare building with buying.

1.title: Assessing the System You Chose: What Is Different Now
1.text: In module eight you assessed a planned use case. Now you assess the system that was actually selected. The table shows the difference: when, what is assessed, the evidence, and who does it. The assessment now covers your use, your people and your data, which the provider's assessment cannot cover. Evidence comes from the provider's documents and your own tests and pilots. The result feeds a go, go with conditions or no-go decision. Exam tip: the provider assesses the product; the deployer assesses the use.

1.title: Gathering the Evidence: Provider Documents and Your Own Tests
1.text: Gather evidence from five sources. Instructions for use under Article thirteen: intended purpose, limits, oversight measures and logs. The model or system card: performance by group and evaluation conditions. Test, audit and certification reports, and any provider risk assessment. And your own pilot and test results on your data and users. Gaps are findings: missing documents, vague claims and untested conditions go on the risk list. Ask the provider in writing. Exam tip: treat provider documents as claims to check against your own tests, not as proof.

1.title: Deployer Duties That Feed the Assessment
1.text: For high-risk systems, Article twenty-six sets deployer duties. Use the system as the instructions say, assign human oversight to people with competence, training and authority, and check that input data are relevant and representative. Monitor, inform the provider, suspend use if there is a risk, and report any serious incident. Keep logs for at least six months, and tell workers and affected people. Article twenty-seven adds a fundamental rights impact assessment for certain deployers, and it may cross-refer to a data protection impact assessment. Exam tip: Article twenty-six applies to every deployer of a high-risk system; Article twenty-seven reaches only certain deployers.

1.title: Reviewing an Existing Assessment
1.text: Sometimes the task is to review an assessment that already exists: the provider's, a predecessor's, or an earlier version. Ask six questions. Is it current? Is the scope right for your use, people and setting? Is there evidence, not only claims? Does it cover affected groups, including vulnerable people? Do mitigations have owners and dates? And does it name triggers for reassessment? Reuse what holds, fill the gaps, and record what changed. Exam tip: a reused assessment is acceptable only if it matches your use; otherwise update it.

1.title: Helios: The Impact Assessment on the Chosen Assistant
1.text: Here is the assessment at Helios. Scope: the Corvid Labs model, used through an interface, grounded on Helios's support documents, answering customers in public chat. Findings: wrong or outdated answers can harm customers and trust; chats may hold personal data; some customers may be vulnerable or rely on an answer. Conditions for go: owners and review dates for the support documents; the assistant says when it does not know and offers a person; a monitoring and incident plan; and trained support staff. The decision is go with conditions. Exam tip: the output is a decision with conditions, not a score.

1.title: Why the Contract Is a Governance Control
1.text: A vendor or license agreement is where the provider's promises and limits are written down. It allocates risk between provider and customer, and it is evidence for audits and regulators. It is also the customer's best leverage, because terms are hardest to change after signing. Six families of terms matter: data, intellectual property, security and confidentiality, performance and audit, liability, and change and exit. Review with procurement, legal and privacy, security and the business owner. At Helios, Ravi Menon and Jonas Weber lead. Exam tip: the contract is a governance tool.

1.title: Data Terms: Use, Ownership, Retention and Location
1.text: Data terms come first. May the provider use your prompts and files to train or improve its models? Prefer no, unless you agree. Who owns inputs and outputs, and any fine-tuned version? For personal data, G D P R Article twenty-eight, point three, requires a binding processor contract: documented instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processor conditions, help with data subject requests, deletion or return, and audit information. Under point four, sub-processors are bound by the same obligations, and the first processor stays fully liable. Check retention, deletion and location, and the transfer rules in Articles forty-four to forty-nine. Exam tip: ask whether your inputs train the model.

1.title: Intellectual Property: Ownership, Training Data and Indemnity
1.text: For intellectual property, ask four things. Outputs: who owns or may use what the system produces, and are there restrictions? Training data: does the provider warrant its rights to the training data, as module five discussed? Indemnity: will the provider defend and compensate the customer if the model or its output is said to infringe someone's rights, and which exclusions apply, such as misuse or edited output? And your inputs: your own content must not be reused without permission. General-purpose model providers need a copyright policy and a training-content summary under Article fifty-three, point one. Exam tip: read what the indemnity leaves out.

1.title: Security and Confidentiality Terms
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Security terms start with commitments: access controls, encryption, testing, recognized certifications and a right to see the evidence. Confidentiality means your prompts, files and outputs stay confidential, with limits on staff and sub-processor access. Incident notice needs a fixed, short time. A processor must notify the controller without undue delay, under G D P R Article thirty-three, point two, and your own reporting clocks from module ten can be short. Add protection against prompt injection, data leakage and model theft. Exam tip: the contract must say how fast the vendor must tell you.

1.title: Performance, Documentation and Audit Rights
1.text: The table lists five things to secure. Service levels: availability, response and support times, with remedies if missed. Performance statements: accuracy and limits, ideally by group. Documentation: instructions for use and model information, under Article thirteen, kept current. Testing and audit rights: to test, assess or audit the system, or receive independent reports; a processor must support audits under Article twenty-eight, point three. And cooperation: where a high-risk system is built on a supplier's parts, Article twenty-five, point four, calls for a written agreement on information, capabilities and technical access. Exam tip: without these rights, a customer cannot do its own oversight.

1.title: Liability, Indemnities and Insurance
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Liability terms decide who pays. Liability caps are often limited to the fees paid, so check whether data breach, I P and confidentiality are carved out or have a higher cap. Vendors may exclude losses from errors in A I output, so know what stays with you. Indemnities give defense and payment for named claims, such as I P or data breach caused by the vendor. Contracts allocate loss between the parties; they do not remove duties to regulators or to affected people. Ask about insurance. Exam tip: a cap limits what the vendor pays you, not what you owe to others.

1.title: Change, Notice and Exit
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The agreement has a life: sign, run, change and exit. Model changes are the big issue. The provider may update or replace the model, so require advance notice of material changes, release notes and time to retest, and consider version pinning. Ask how long an old version stays available. For subcontractors and changed terms, require notice and a right to object or leave. For exit, require termination rights, return and deletion of data, transition help and access to logs. At Helios, an unannounced change could invalidate the tests and the impact assessment. Exam tip: write notice and retest time into the contract.

1.title: Weighing the Terms: Red Flags and a Review Checklist
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. When you weigh the terms, look at what each term allocates and what is missing. The table lists six red flags and what to ask for instead. A broad right to train on your data: ask for no training without agreement. No I P indemnity: ask for defense and payment. A cap with no carve-outs: ask for a higher cap. Changes without notice: ask for notice and version pinning. No audit rights: ask for documentation and testing rights. No incident notice: ask for a fixed period. Record accepted gaps, and escalate unresolved high risks. Exam tip: match strictness to the risk of the use.

2.title: Deploying Your Own Model: What Changes
2.text: A proprietary model of your own is one the company develops, or has developed, and runs under its own name. A provider develops an A I system or model and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name, under Article three, point three. Helios today is a deployer. An in-house build would make Helios the provider too, with the developer's duties from modules eight to ten. No vendor stands between you and the user. Putting your name on a high-risk system, or substantially modifying one, also makes you the provider, under Article twenty-five, point one. Exam tip: building moves you to the provider's side.

2.title: More Obligations: The Provider's Duties
2.text: If the system is high-risk, the provider meets the requirements in Articles nine to fifteen: risk management, data governance, documentation, logs, instructions, oversight, accuracy and security. Article sixteen adds a quality management system, under Article seventeen, with documentation and logs. Before release come the conformity assessment, the declaration, the C E marking and registration, in Articles forty-three, forty-seven, forty-eight and forty-nine. After release come post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting, in Articles seventy-two and seventy-three. A general-purpose model adds Article fifty-three, point one. The company also keeps its deployer duties. Exam tip: own model, own duties.

2.title: Higher Potential Liability
2.text: With your own model, there is no vendor to share the blame. Claims about defects, bias or harm come to you as the maker. The new E U Product Liability Directive covers software and A I systems and applies to products placed on the market from the ninth of December, twenty twenty-six. Makers can be liable for defects that appear through updates or machine learning. You also face the regulatory exposure of the A I Act, and contract exposure if your promises exceed what you can deliver. Reduce it with documentation, testing evidence, monitoring, incident handling, insurance and clear terms of use. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, check how the Directive applies before release.

2.title: Opportunities: Control, Fit and Advantage
2.text: Running your own model has real opportunities: control over data, behavior and update timing; a better fit to your domain; ownership of the resulting I P; less dependence on a vendor; possible lower cost at scale; and differentiation. But the costs and duties arrive together: the provider's obligations, higher liability, specialist talent and infrastructure, ongoing retraining and monitoring, and security of weights and data. Weigh both. At Helios, an in-house assistant could keep data inside the company, but Helios would need new skills and a quality management system. Exam tip: control comes with accountability.

2.title: Build, Buy or Both: Deciding With Eyes Open
2.text: The table compares four routes. Buy: the fastest start, the provider carries the build duties, and the contract is your main control. Host an open model: more control, but you take on hosting, security, testing and updates. Build: the most control and fit, but all provider duties and liability. Hybrid: a base model plus your data or retrieval, where you must check whether the changes make you a provider. Decide with requirements, risk, skills, cost, time and the committee's risk appetite, and record the decision. At Helios: go with conditions, with no in-house build until staffing, a quality management system and budget are in place.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Assess the chosen system: your use, people and data, using provider documents plus your own tests, the Article twenty-six and twenty-seven duties, and a review of existing assessments for currency and fit. Vendor terms: data use, I P and indemnity, security and incident notice, performance and audit rights, liability, and change and exit, and know the red flags. Your own model: you become the provider, with more obligations, higher liability, and more control. And decide: build, buy or both, with the decision recorded.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Helios has selected the Corvid Labs model for its customer assistant. The design-stage impact assessment assumed an internal-only tool, but the assistant will now answer customers in public chat. What should the governance lead do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The deployer assesses its own use of the chosen system. Public use is a material change, so update the assessment before launch.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A company reviews an impact assessment written by the provider of a hiring tool before relying on it. Which two checks are most useful? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. A reused assessment must be current and match the deployer's use, and its mitigations need owners, dates and reassessment triggers. Layout and length say nothing about quality.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A company reviews a vendor's generative A I service agreement. Which term most directly addresses the risk that employees' confidential prompts could be used to train the vendor's model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Data terms control whether prompts and files may be reused. Uptime, courts and invoice dates matter to the contract, but none stops training on the customer's inputs.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Ravi Menon and Jonas Weber review the Corvid Labs agreement. It lets the vendor replace the model at any time without notice. What is the main risk, and the best fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A silent model change can invalidate the tests and the impact assessment. The contract should require notice, time to retest, and the option to stay on a tested version.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Which two terms in an A I vendor agreement best help the customer meet its own oversight and assessment duties? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Oversight and assessment need documentation, the right to test or audit, and fast notice of incidents. Ownership of the customer's inputs, logo rights and the vendor's head office do not help.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A company that uses a vendor's A I system decides to build its own proprietary model for the same purpose. Which statement about its position is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The company becomes the provider, with the developer's obligations and a greater share of the liability. Building a model does not lower the duties or take the system outside the law.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: D. Question two: C and E. Question three: A. Question four: B. Question five: B and D. Question six: C. That completes Module twelve. Next, Module thirteen: governing deployment and use, with oversight, monitoring, unintended uses, communication, and the policy to deactivate or localize a system.
